_status: Module 2 questions match the Module 2 deck's recall slide (synced 20 October 2026). Modules 3 and 4 follow their learner guides (21 October 2026): Module 3 opens with a recap of Day 1, Module 4 with a recall of this morning. Module 5 is a draft.

questions.q: The portal is locked by ransomware. Secret, Correct or Ready?
A breach must be reported when three things are true. Which three?
Notify within how many hours? Full report within how many days?
questions.a: **72-5:** 72 hours to notify; full report within 5 days from discovery.

questions.q: Name the four threat modeling questions.
questions.a: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job?

questions.q: What do the letters in SLAM stand for?
Ben wants 2,500 applicant records on a USB stick at home. What does Sec. 23 require?
questions.a: **Clearance, approval, 1,000, encrypt:** the head's approval, at most 1,000 records at a time, encrypted. 2,500 is too many.

questions.q: A firewall reads its rules in what order?
questions.a: From the top: **the first rule that matches decides**; everything else falls to the default deny.

questions.q: Lock, seal, sign: which one proves who sent a file?
questions.a: **Sign:** a digital signature, checked with the sender's public key.

questions.q: Why does a security key resist phishing when an SMS code does not?
questions.a: It checks the real site's address and will not sign in to a fake page.

questions.q: Two hands on money: give one RSSO example.
questions.a: Whoever edits an e-wallet number cannot release the payout.
At **reasonable belief**: smell smoke, not ashes.

questions.q: Which goal does ransomware hit first?
questions.a: **Ready** (availability), often Secret too when data is stolen.

questions.q: A padlock in the address bar means what?
questions.a: The connection is encrypted. It does **not** mean the site is trustworthy.
